Imagine a spider's web thread — it exists, yes, but it is so thin and fragile that the slightest disturbance could break it completely. That mental image is the heart of tenuous. Something tenuous is barely there, very weak, and likely to fall apart easily. It lacks strength, substance, or solid foundation.

The opposite of tenuous is something strong, firm, and solid — something you can depend on. Tenuous is the opposite of that.

Tenuous almost always describes one of two things:

1. A connection or relationship between things
This is the most common use. When two things are connected, but only barely — the connection is so indirect, thin, or weak that you could almost argue they aren't really connected at all — that connection is tenuous.

"The detective's case rested on a tenuous link between the suspect and the crime scene — just a single, blurry photograph."

The link exists, but it's fragile. A good lawyer could knock it down easily.

2. An argument, claim, belief, or position
When someone makes a claim but has very little evidence or logical support for it, that claim is tenuous. You're not saying it's completely wrong — you're saying it barely holds up.

"His argument that exercise has no health benefits is, at best, tenuous."

It doesn't have the weight of strong evidence behind it. It's shaky.
The Key Feeling of the Word

"Tenuous" carries a feeling of fragility and uncertainty. When you call something tenuous, you are gently (or pointedly) signalling that:

  • It could collapse under the slightest pressure.
  • It doesn't have much supporting it.
  • You wouldn't want to bet heavily on it.
  • It appears to exist or hold, but barely.

It is often used to express polite scepticism or careful doubt. Rather than saying "that's wrong," you say "that connection seems tenuous" — which is a more measured, intelligent way of questioning something.
Common Pairings (What It Describes Most Often)

Here are the words that most naturally sit next to tenuous in real usage:

  • Tenuous connection / link / relationship — barely any real relationship between two things
  • Tenuous argument / case / claim — an argument with very little backing
  • Tenuous evidence — evidence that is weak or barely sufficient
  • Tenuous grip / hold — a hold on something that could slip at any moment
  • Tenuous position — a situation that is unstable and easily threatened
  • Tenuous thread — often used figuratively, like "hanging by a tenuous thread," meaning something is barely surviving

"She had a tenuous grasp of the material — she understood the basics, but one tough question would have exposed her."

"The company's financial position was tenuous after years of losses."

"Critics argued that the film's plot relied on tenuous coincidences that no real person would believe."

"Their friendship had become tenuous over the years, barely surviving on occasional text messages."

"There is only a tenuous connection between the two events — they happened in the same city, but little else links them."

It does not mean "fake" or "non-existent." Something tenuous still exists — it's just barely there. If a connection is tenuous, there is a connection, but a very weak one. This is an important distinction. You wouldn't call something tenuous if it didn't exist at all.

It is not the same as "temporary." Something tenuous is weak, not necessarily short-lived. (Though something tenuous often becomes short-lived, because weak things tend to break.)

Words with a similar meaning: weak, flimsy, fragile, thin, slight, shaky, questionable, insubstantial, precarious, slim, dubious.

Words with the opposite meaning: strong, solid, firm, substantial, robust, well-founded, convincing, stable.

Among the synonyms, tenuous is the most elegant and precise choice when you want to describe something as barely holding together intellectually or logically. "Flimsy" sounds more casual and dismissive. "Shaky" sounds more emotional. Tenuous sounds measured and analytical, which is why it appears often in formal writing, journalism, legal analysis, and academic discussions.
The Subtle Register of This Word

Tenuous is a word that educated, careful speakers use. When someone calls an argument "tenuous," they are being precise — they're not saying it's nonsense, they're saying it lacks the foundation needed to stand firmly. It's a word of careful, intelligent criticism. Using it signals that you have thought critically about something rather than just dismissing it emotionally.
Tenuous = barely there, weak, and likely to fall apart — whether you're talking about a connection between ideas, a piece of evidence, an argument, or a hold on a situation.
